file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** of how to create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that boots Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and attaches an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (if that GPU type is available in your region).  
The example uses the **REST API** (via `curl`) and also shows the equivalent `gcloud` command for convenience.

> ⚠️ **Important**  
> * Google Cloud does **not** use the term “EC2”; that’s Amazon Web Services.  
> * The RTX A6000 is not a standard GCP GPU type.  GCP offers GPUs such as `nvidia-tesla-a100`, `nvidia-tesla-v100`, `nvidia-tesla-t4`, etc.  
> * If you really need an RTX A6000, you’ll have to check whether your region supports it or use a custom image that contains the driver.  
> * The example below assumes you have a project ID (`YOUR_PROJECT_ID`), a zone (`YOUR_ZONE`), and a valid OAuth 2.0 access token (`YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN`).  

---

## 1.  REST API Call (curl)

```bash
# Variables – replace with your own values
PROJECT_ID="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
ZONE="YOUR_ZONE"          # e.g., us-central1-a
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"
ACCESS_TOKEN="YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN"

# JSON payload
read -r -d '' INSTANCE_BODY <<EOF
{
  "name": "$INSTANCE_NAME",
  "machineType": "zones/$ZONE/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/ubuntu-2004-focal-v20230912"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "scheduling": {
    "preemptible": false,
    "automaticRestart": true
  },
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorType": "projects/$PROJECT_ID/zones/$ZONE/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a6000",
      "acceleratorCount": 1
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": [
        "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
EOF

# Make the API request
curl -X POST \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/zones/$ZONE/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$INSTANCE_BODY"
```

### What the payload does

| Field | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `name` | Instance name |
| `machineType` | CPU & memory (here `n1-standard-8` – 8 vCPUs, 30 GB RAM) |
| `disks[0]` | Boot disk, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `networkInterfaces[0]` | Default VPC + external IP |
| `scheduling` | Non‑preemptible, auto‑restart |
| `guestAccelerators[0]` | Attach one RTX A6000 GPU |
| `serviceAccounts[0]` | Default service account with full cloud scope |

> **Tip:** If the GPU type `nvidia-tesla-a6000` is not available, replace it with a supported type (e.g., `nvidia-tesla-a100`).

---

## 2.  Equivalent `gcloud` Command

If you prefer the CLI, the same instance can be created with:

```bash
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --machine-type="n1-standard-8" \
  --image-project="ubuntu-os-cloud" \
  --image-family="ubuntu-2004-lts" \
  --boot-disk-size=50GB \
  --accelerator="type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1" \
  --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
  --restart-on-failure
```

> *The `--image-family` flag automatically pulls the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image.*

---

## 3.  Prerequisites Checklist

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Enable the **Compute Engine API** in your project. |
| 2 | Ensure you have **billing enabled** and the project has enough quota for GPUs in the chosen zone. |
| 3 | Create an **OAuth 2.0 access token** with the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` scope (or use a service account key). |
| 4 | Verify that the **GPU type** you want is available in your zone (`gcloud compute accelerator-types list --zone=$ZONE`). |
| 5 | Run the `curl` or `gcloud` command above. |

---

## 4.  Quick Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| `404 Not Found` on the accelerator type | GPU type not available in zone | Check with `gcloud compute accelerator-types list` |
| `403 Forbidden` | Insufficient permissions | Grant the service account the required scopes or use a user with the right IAM role |
| `Quota exceeded` | GPU quota reached | Request a quota increase in the Cloud Console |

---

### Final Note

Once the instance is created, you’ll need to install the NVIDIA drivers and CUDA toolkit manually (or use a custom image that already contains them). GCP provides a **GPU driver installer** script that can be run after the instance boots:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535
```

(Replace `535` with the driver version that matches your GPU.)

Happy GPU computing! 🚀
